query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under controlled high‐temperature exposure, the degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA is governed by two competing microstructural pathways that depend on the ambient gas. In an O2‐rich atmosphere, selective oxidation of reactive elements, especially Cr and Ti, occurs preferentially along the grain boundaries. This leads to the formation of brittle oxide phases that cause intergranular embrittlement and eventually catastrophic failure. In a reducing gas environment, the absence of a protective oxide layer promotes internal elemental redistribution and phase segregation (or dealloying) within the FCC matrix, destabilizing the microstructure and similarly predisposing the material to failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a homogeneous FCC matrix containing inherent residual stresses, fine microstructural features, and minor inclusions from the AM process.
generation.intervention: A controlled gas environment switch experiment where the sample, heated to approximately 900 °C, is first held in an oxidizing (O2‐rich) atmosphere and then rapidly switched to a reducing (H2‐ or CO‐rich) atmosphere, with continuous in situ monitoring (e.g., high-temperature XRD and microscopy).
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure within the 700–1100 °C range. The experiment starts with an oxidizing environment to promote grain-boundary oxidation, followed by a switch to a reducing atmosphere to evaluate the onset of internal phase segregation, all under well-controlled gas compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of microstructural features at the grain boundaries (oxidation-induced brittle phases) versus the development of internal phase segregation or dealloying within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: In O2-rich conditions, reactive elements (particularly Cr and Ti) oxidize selectively at grain boundaries, forming brittle oxide precipitates that weaken intergranular cohesion. In reducing conditions, the lack of a substantial oxide layer results in abnormal elemental redistribution, triggering phase segregation within the FCC matrix. Both pathways deteriorate the mechanical integrity by undermining the cohesive properties essential for resisting catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: During a controlled gas switch at ~900 °C, samples maintained in an oxidizing environment will show early and detectable formation of grain-boundary oxide phases (via characteristic diffraction peaks and micro-imaging) and evidence of intergranular cracks. In contrast, samples exposed to a reducing atmosphere after the switch will display pronounced internal phase segregation or dealloying signatures within the FCC matrix with minimal grain-boundary oxidation, diverging notably from the as-fabricated homogeneous baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated additively manufactured alloy featuring a homogeneous FCC matrix with minimal oxidation and phase segregation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-temperature exposures between 700 and 1100 °C under strictly controlled oxidizing and reducing atmospheres. Deviations outside this temperature window or in non-controlled environments might yield different degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide formation versus phase segregation and the quantitative mechanical degradation differences between the two environments remain uncertain without further detailed experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform an in situ gas-switch experiment at ~900 °C. Prepare two sets of samples: one continuously exposed to an oxidizing (O2-rich) atmosphere and another where the atmosphere is initially O2-rich and then switched to a reducing (H2- or CO-rich) environment. Continuously monitor microstructural evolution using high-temperature XRD and real-time microscopy.
measurements: Detection of grain-boundary oxidation (e.g., appearance of specific oxide diffraction peaks and imaging of oxide precipitates).
Identification of internal phase segregation or dealloying within the FCC matrix (via emergence of secondary phase peaks or compositional mapping changes).
Post-exposure mechanical testing (e.g., microhardness and fracture toughness) to correlate microstructural changes with embrittlement.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the gas-switch experiment fails to show distinct differences in microstructural evolution between the oxidizing and reducing conditions. Specifically, if neither significant grain-boundary oxidation nor clear internal phase segregation is observed relative to the as-fabricated baseline—or if both conditions produce indistinguishable degradation patterns—then the proposed mechanism linking ambient gas conditions to distinct degradation behaviors leading to catastrophic failure is not supported.

The high entropy alloy (HEA) of equiatomic composition CrNiFeCoMn and with FCC crystal structure was additively manufactured in a selective laser melting (SLM) process starting from mechanically alloyed powders. The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K. The precipitates increase in number and dimensions after long-period annealing at 900–1300 K, with a change in the HEA mechanical properties. Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries, but still with the presence of a finer Cr-rich nitride precipitation phase. These results suggest that the as-produced HEA is a supersaturated solid solution at low and intermediate temperature with nitrides and σ nanostructures.

AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. frame.system: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix in its as‐fabricated state (including potential residual stresses, fine microstructural features, and minor inclusions from the AM process).
frame.goal: To identify and mechanistically explain the degradation pathways under elevated-temperature exposure and understand why catastrophic failure might occur under oxidizing versus reducing gas conditions.
frame.limitation: A lack of detailed mechanistic understanding linking surface or microstructural changes (e.g., selective oxidation, phase segregation) during high-temperature exposure to the onset of catastrophic failure.
constraints: must propose a testable mechanistic hypothesis
specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior
provide predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline
frame.regime: Elevated-temperature conditions (for example, within a 700–1100 °C range) under controlled atmospheres of oxidizing (e.g., O2-rich) and reducing (e.g., H2- or CO-rich) gases.
prior_attempts: Previous investigations have correlated surface oxidation with performance loss but did not directly link microstructural degradation (e.g., intergranular oxidation or phase segregation) to catastrophic failure.
Studies using post-exposure fractography or ex-situ analysis that did not implement controlled, gas-composition switches to isolate the effects of oxidizing versus reducing environments.
frame.understanding: The emerging hypothesis is that under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation of elements like Cr and Ti at grain boundaries leads to the formation of brittle oxide phases, triggering localized embrittlement and intergranular cracking. In contrast, reducing environments may suppress the formation of protective oxide layers but promote internal dealloying or phase segregation, destabilizing the FCC matrix. This microstructural instability, in combination with residual stresses inherent from additive manufacturing, sets the stage for catastrophic failure. A controlled experimental change—switching the prevailing gas environment at a critical temperature—should reveal these competing mechanisms. If, upon switching atmospheres, one observes a marked initiation of intergranular oxidation or phase changes (via in-situ microscopy or diffraction methods) relative to the baseline state, this supports the hypothesis. Conversely, failure to detect these microstructural transitions under the prescribed exposure conditions would falsify the proposed mechanism.

decision.trend: Early work on high‐entropy alloys in high‐temperature environments first established that oxidation kinetics (typically following parabolic rate laws) and the formation of oxide scales can degrade the alloy’s integrity (PMC8346963). Subsequent atomistic simulation studies (PMC9969177) linked chemical surface reactions—in particular, selective oxidation occurring at grain boundaries—with shifts in the operative deformation mechanisms and even phase transformation. In both cases, the studies noted microstructural evolution (e.g., intergranular oxide formation or phase instability) as a precursor to mechanical degradation. However, while the first generation of studies associated overall performance loss with oxidation, later works hinted that the exact microstructural pathways leading to catastrophic failure (whether through intergranular embrittlement or dealloying/phase segregation) would critically depend on the ambient gas (oxidizing versus reducing).
decision.unsolved: A controlled, in-situ experiment isolating the effect of a gas environment switch on microstructural evolution in additively manufactured FCC high-entropy alloys has not been performed. Specifically, it remains unproven whether switching between oxidizing and reducing atmospheres at a defined critical temperature can distinctly trigger either intergranular selective oxidation (leading to embrittlement) or suppress protective oxide layer formation in favor of internal phase segregation, thereby directly linking these processes with the onset of catastrophic failure.
decision.lever: Implement a gas environment switch experiment by transitioning from an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., O2-rich) to a reducing gas (e.g., H2- or CO-rich) at a critical high temperature (e.g., near 900 °C) during in-situ exposure with real-time diffraction/microscopy monitoring.
decision.why: This approach follows the evolving trend where oxidation-induced microstructural changes at grain boundaries have been linked to degradation, while reducing conditions are predicted to promote internal phase segregation. Switching the controlled atmosphere in-situ will enable a direct observation of which mechanism dominates the degradation process and under what conditions catastrophic failure is triggered, thus providing a clear testable mechanistic hypothesis with an unambiguous falsification criterion.
